messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Hopelessness: I have no future, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
Malia, a 53-year-old widowed shopowner of Pacific Islander heritage, came to treatment after more than a year of feeling as though the ground beneath her life had never settled back into place. Before her husband died, she had run their small neighborhood shop with him, taking pride in the steady routines of serving regular customers and closing the store together at the end of the day. His death had been sudden and unexpected, and what remained with her was not a neat recollection but a jagged sequence that refused to organize itself into a story. She could recall fragments in a way that made her uneasy even to think about: the look of things, the shock of the moment, the sense that everything had turned unreal. When she tried to speak about it, she found that the account would not come out clearly even to herself. She would start, stop, and then circle back, as if she were trying to describe something she had seen through shattered glass. In her mind the event played over and over like a film that she could not turn off, the same scenes returning without her asking for them, forcing their way into her mind at work, at home, and even while she was trying to sleep.

In the months after the death, Malia began to notice that certain moments brought the loss back with a force that startled her. When people talked about someone losing a loved one, she would suddenly go still, her attention pulled away from the conversation and toward the memory she was trying not to enter. Funerals, cemeteries, and grief-related events were especially difficult; the sight of a memorial display or even hearing that someone was attending a service could make her chest tighten and her mind race ahead to the moment she had lost her husband. Alcohol smell was another powerful trigger. If a customer came into the shop smelling of alcohol, or if she caught the odor lingering on someone near the counter, she would feel immediately unsettled, as if something bad were about to happen. At those moments she often reacted as though there were danger in the room, even when nothing was actually wrong. She would scan the space quickly, her body tense and ready, unable to relax even in familiar, safe places. She was aware, on one level, that she was standing in her own shop or sitting in her own kitchen, but another part of her responded as if she were back in the worst moment, suddenly feeling and acting as though the death were happening all over again.

Malia’s days became organized around keeping herself from being overwhelmed by these moments, though she did not describe it in those terms. She found herself avoiding funerals and cemeteries, staying away from grief-related gatherings that other family members attended, and making excuses when conversations turned to other people’s losses. In her shop she learned to step back from customers who smelled of alcohol, handing off interactions when she could, because the smell could pull her into the memory before she had time to prepare herself. These were practical choices at first, but they changed the texture of her life. She became more withdrawn in the very place that had once been central to her identity, spending less time chatting with customers and more time waiting for the next jolt of fear or the next unwelcome image to arrive. The business still needed to be opened, stocked, and kept going, but she often moved through the day with a sense of strain, as though she were holding herself together by force.

What distressed Malia most was not only the returning memory but what the loss seemed to have done to her sense of who she was. She had come to believe that she did not know herself anymore. The woman who once moved through life with confidence in her role as wife, partner, and shopkeeper now felt unfamiliar to herself, as if that person had died alongside her husband. She spoke with a flat certainty that her life had been destroyed by the trauma and that she had no future. This was not a passing sadness to her but a conviction that colored nearly everything she said about the years ahead. She described herself as living in the shadow of what had happened, unable to picture a version of life that would feel whole again. Even in calm moments she could not settle; the feeling of danger could rise without warning, and she remained braced for another surge of the memory, another flash of the moment when the world changed.

She finally sought help because the relentless replay, the sudden false alarms in ordinary settings, and the sense that her life had ended with her husband’s death were no longer something she could keep managing alone. What she most hoped for was some relief from the way the memory invaded her and some way of feeling like herself again, though she was also afraid that nothing would change and that the future she could not imagine would remain forever out of reach.
